entries.clue: Companion enters hospital department in pain (4)

indicatorNotes.enters: the companion goes into the department, so CH sits inside A&E

blocks.note: A&E, the accident and emergency department

annotation.surface: A hospital visitor walks into casualty in agony.
annotation.walkthrough: A&E is the British name for the emergency room; the ampersand simply drops out of the grid.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: a dull lasting hurt, such as toothache, is a kind of pain.

entries.clue: Trip to arrive in mountainous area (8)

blocks.note: a drug trip is a high

annotation.surface: A traveller's journey ends somewhere in the hills.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Trip' reads as a journey, fitting the arrival, but it is the drugs sense that gives HIGH.
annotation.definitionFit: A region of elevated ground and hills, as in the Scottish uplands, is described by this word.

indicatorNotes.in: the ring is placed in the memory

annotation.surface: A ring kept in memory of someone lost.
annotation.walkthrough: The definition is a cross-reference: 13 down is SPACE.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym for capacity, as in 'no room to move' meaning there is no free area left.

blocks.note: each 3 points to 3 down, a place to live; several together make lodgings
each 1/4 is one of four equal parts

annotation.surface: A little sum that looks like broken arithmetic.
annotation.walkthrough: The first 3 is not a number but a cross-reference to 3 down, ROOM; several rooms are living quarters. The equation looks false until both sides are read as words.
annotation.definitionFit: Soldiers' lodgings are made of rooms, and each fraction of one fourth is also named by this word.

entries.clue: Last one standing carries lots of weight (6)

indicatorNotes.carries: the phrase holds the answer within its letters

annotation.surface: The final survivor of a contest is carrying a heavy load.
annotation.walkthrough: A stone is an imperial weight of 14 pounds, still used in Britain for body weight.
annotation.definitionFit: Each is an imperial unit of fourteen pounds, so several of them add up to plenty.

indicatorNotes.broken: the letters are broken apart and rebuilt

annotation.surface: A silver wax seal found cracked inside a royal residence.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Seal' looks like a wax stamp or an animal, but the two words just supply ten letters, and 'broken' tells you to rebuild them.
annotation.definitionFit: Louis XIV's vast royal residence outside Paris is the best-known example of the kind.

indicatorNotes.defending: the country guards, so surrounds, the other letters
indicatorNotes.rambling: the letters of MAN'S wander out of order

annotation.surface: A nation shields a man whose talk wanders, and someone wants him exposed.
annotation.walkthrough: The two letters for the country split to surround the rearranged MAN'S; the apostrophe is surface punctuation.
annotation.definitionFit: Taking off a disguise reveals the person beneath, so the word extends to revealing any hidden truth.

indicatorNotes.Discovering: read as dis-covering: take the covers, the outer letters, off each word

annotation.surface: Finding out that they have been promoted to boss.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Discovering' looks like finding out; split it as dis-covering and it strips each word of its ends.
annotation.definitionFit: The person at the top of a school, company or family is its chief, so the word stands for anyone in charge.

indicatorNotes.into: the look goes into the firm

blocks.note: an air is a look or manner

annotation.surface: An instruction to investigate a company's funds.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Capital' reads as the firm's money, but it is a capital city.
annotation.definitionFit: A capital here is a seat of government; this one is Egypt's, on the Nile.

entries.clue: ‘Increase risk from chopped peanut’ – inspiring article (2,3,4)

indicatorNotes.chopped: the peanut is cut up and reassembled
indicatorNotes.inspiring: breathing in, so taking the article inside

annotation.surface: A food-allergy warning about chopped nuts.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface reads as an allergy warning, but 'Increase risk' is the definition. The ante is the stake each poker player puts in before a hand.
annotation.definitionFit: A poker idiom: raising the stake each player must put in makes the game more dangerous.

entries.clue: Record bird circling me – it won’t last long (9)

indicatorNotes.circling: a bird circling something flies round it, so HERON goes round ME

annotation.surface: A bird flying round the speaker, with a note that it is short-lived.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Record' reads as a verb, noting the bird down; it is a noun, the EP. The definition is a whole phrase describing the answer.
annotation.definitionFit: From Greek for 'lasting a day', it names something short-lived, such as a mayfly.

blocks.note: to sand is to polish a surface

annotation.surface: A language lesson: the Polish word for time also means resistance.
annotation.walkthrough: The capital P makes it look like the language; it is polish, the verb.
annotation.definitionFit: Holding out against an attack is called making one, so the noun means opposition or refusal to give way.

entries.clue: Perhaps the Sun let being hacked shock (7)

indicatorNotes.Perhaps: the Sun is one example of a star
indicatorNotes.being hacked: LET is chopped up and rearranged

annotation.surface: Maybe the tabloid allowed phone hacking, to general shock.
annotation.walkthrough: The Sun reads as the British tabloid newspaper, tying in with hacking; here it is the star.
annotation.definitionFit: A sudden fright makes someone jump, which is what shocking them does.

blocks.note: a spa is a mineral spring or well

annotation.surface: A remark that a church is building something without any charm.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Well' looks like a throat-clearing opener; it is a spring. On a keyboard a space is typed like a character but shows nothing.
annotation.definitionFit: In typed text this is the blank gap between words, where no visible letter or symbol appears.

entries.clue: Stealing fancy store jewellery – you involved? (10)

indicatorNotes.fancy: the store's letters are dressed up in a new order
indicatorNotes.involved: you is caught up inside them

blocks.note: U sounds like you, as in text speak

annotation.surface: An accusation of shoplifting from a smart jeweller's.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fancy' reads as posh, describing the store; it tells you to rearrange. To trouser is British slang for pocketing money, often dishonestly.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang: putting something in your pocket, especially money you should not have, is pocketing it for yourself.

entries.clue: Dagger, not a dessert, smuggled into prison (7)

indicatorNotes.not: 'not a' tells you the letter A is absent from the dessert that follows
indicatorNotes.smuggled into: the dessert is slipped inside the prison

annotation.surface: A blade hidden in a cake is smuggled into jail, the old file-in-the-cake trick.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Not a' removes the letter A from CAKE, which then sits inside STIR.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that sticks or stabs, so a knife used for killing pigs or a blade in general.

indicatorNotes.Soundly: the answer is heard, not spelt, like the twists

blocks.note: to wrest is to twist or wrench

annotation.surface: Someone expertly bends the kit on a snooker table.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Soundly' looks like 'thoroughly'; it signals sound. Snooker is a British cue game, and a rest supports the cue for long shots.
annotation.definitionFit: These are cross-headed sticks that hold up a player's cue for shots out of reach.

blocks.note: a wheel is round, like O

annotation.surface: Asking whether a car with a single wheel is roadworthy.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sound?' looks like asking whether the car is safe; it means audio.
annotation.definitionFit: The word comes from Latin for 'I hear' and names recorded or broadcast noise as opposed to pictures.

indicatorNotes.50% off: a sale reduction of half, so half the word's letters are taken off

blocks.note: SETTEE, a sofa, with its back half removed

annotation.surface: An advert for a half-price sofa with a firm cushion.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Firm' looks like an adjective describing the sofa, and it is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: Something that has hardened, such as concrete or jelly, is solid and fixed.

indicatorNotes.rewound: played backwards, as with a recording
indicatorNotes.during: the turned letters sit within the other word

annotation.surface: A football video referee replays a moment when a short cross came in.
annotation.walkthrough: VAR is the video assistant referee in football. 'Short cross' reads as a pass; 'short' is TERSE and 'cross' is the definition.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: to go across something, like a climber moving sideways over a rock face.

blocks.note: British slang for hitting someone hard

annotation.surface: Blows to the face cause black eyes.
annotation.walkthrough: A shiner is a black eye, so the surface is a boxing truism; here shiners are things that shine.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for hitting someone hard, and also lights such as table or street fittings that glow.

entries.clue: Film on extremely serious Lady Hamilton? (8)

indicatorNotes.extremely: only the extremes of the word, its end letters

annotation.surface: A deadly serious film about Emma Hamilton.
annotation.walkthrough: The question mark flags Lady Hamilton as one example rather than a synonym.
annotation.definitionFit: Emma Hamilton was Admiral Nelson's lover, a famous example of a kept woman.

entries.clue: Clasp them briefly with heaving moobs (7)

indicatorNotes.briefly: said briefly, the word is clipped the way speech clips it to 'em
indicatorNotes.heaving: the moobs heave, and their letters shift

annotation.surface: A comic hug with a man's heaving chest.
annotation.walkthrough: Moobs is jokey British slang for a man's flabby breasts, and it rearranges to BOSOM.
annotation.definitionFit: An old literary verb for holding someone close to your chest in an embrace.

entries.clue: Don’t allow mirrored license plate with old car (6)

indicatorNotes.mirrored: a mirror shows it back to front

blocks.note: REG, short for registration plate, turned round

annotation.surface: A rule against back-to-front number plates on old cars.
annotation.walkthrough: A banger is British slang for a battered old car.
annotation.definitionFit: British slang for a battered vehicle, named for the backfiring noises it makes.

indicatorNotes.to change gender: F for female becomes M for male

annotation.surface: Asking whether a monarch would switch gender more quickly.
annotation.walkthrough: F and M are the standard abbreviations for female and male, so changing gender swaps one letter for the other.
annotation.definitionFit: One who holds command over servants, animals or a household governs them.

entries.clue: Helps donkey get first and second (7)

annotation.surface: A helpful donkey takes first and second place.
annotation.walkthrough: 'First and second' reads like race placings; they are separate pieces.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: lending a hand or supporting someone in a task, both verbs in the third person.

entries.clue: Ship to remain without any goods (5)

indicatorNotes.without: without means lacking, so the good is taken out of the word

annotation.surface: A cargo ship sitting in port empty.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Goods' looks like cargo, fitting the ship; it stands for G.
annotation.definitionFit: An ocean vessel running a regular route, named for the shipping line that operates it.

indicatorNotes.missing: the police are missing the work, so it is subtracted from them
indicatorNotes.over: the work is turned over before it goes

blocks.note: OP, an opus or work, turned round, and removed

annotation.surface: Police have skipped their job because of surveillance devices.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Bugs' reads as listening devices, fitting cops; here they are insects.
annotation.definitionFit: Small parasitic insects living in hair, loosely grouped with other creepy-crawlies in everyday speech.

indicatorNotes.play: the letters are played with and rearranged

annotation.surface: Asking whether an older relative has to play some instrument.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Play' looks like the verb the elder must do; it is the anagram signal, and 'this instrument' points at the letters just rearranged.
annotation.definitionFit: Trinidad's pan, a tuned percussion piece hammered from an oil barrel, is played with sticks.

entries.clue: South of the border, we’re told lake is secure (4)

indicatorNotes.South of the border: it tells you whose pronunciation to hear: English, not Scottish
indicatorNotes.we’re told: being told something means hearing it

blocks.note: a Scottish lake, as said in England

annotation.surface: A claim from over the Scottish border that a lake is safe.
annotation.walkthrough: 'South of the border' means in England, where people say loch without the Scottish throat sound.
annotation.definitionFit: Fastening a door with a key makes it safe, so the verb means make safe.

indicatorNotes.up: in a down clue, read upwards
indicatorNotes.inside: the answer sits within the words

annotation.surface: An informer who plants evidence, grassing someone up.
annotation.walkthrough: To grass someone up is British slang for informing on them; 'Plant' and 'grasses' pretend to be botany or spying.
annotation.definitionFit: A small flowerless green growth found on stones and trees, which botanists class among the simplest.

entries.clue: Not half clever getting solutions without soap? (9)

annotation.definitionNote: soap is one example; the answer is the plural class it belongs to

indicatorNotes.without: read as without W, W being the abbreviation for with

blocks.note: ANSWERS with the W for with removed

annotation.surface: Someone half-smart is left with answers but no soap.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Without soap' looks like one phrase; split it, since 'without' does the deleting and 'soap?' is the definition by example.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example, flagged by the question mark: soap belongs to the group of products used for washing.

blocks.note: instances, as in 'a case in point'

annotation.walkthrough: Two plain senses joined by 'of'; the surface is barely a picture, so the trick is simply spotting the shared word.
annotation.definitionFit: Instances of something, as in a legal precedent, and also suitcases carried when travelling.
